subject: physics

moments.title: Dirac equation
moments.body:
Dirac writes down a relativistic wave equation for the electron. The equation automatically incorporates spin and predicts the existence of antimatter — the positron, discovered by Carl Anderson in 1932.

The equation has infinities. Calculations of small corrections (like the electron's anomalous magnetic moment) diverge to infinity. Quantum electrodynamics is born but plagued by infinities for two decades.
moments.takeaway: Relativistic quantum theory exists but doesn't yet compute finite answers.

moments.title: Shelter Island Conference
moments.body:
A small conference at Shelter Island brings together America's leading physicists to discuss postwar problems in physics. Two new precision measurements force the issue: the Lamb shift (Willis Lamb's measurement of a tiny shift in hydrogen energy levels) and the electron's anomalous magnetic moment (Rabi's group).

Both need a theory that can calculate finite results from QED.
moments.takeaway: The experimental challenge is laid. Theory must respond.

moments.title: Renormalisation by three independent paths
moments.body:
Three independent formulations of renormalisable QED appear within months. Tomonaga (Tokyo) and Schwinger (Harvard) use canonical methods. Feynman (Cornell) develops his sum-over-histories formulation and the famous diagrams.

Freeman Dyson (Cornell, then IAS) shows the three formulations are equivalent. The infinities can be systematically absorbed into renormalised mass and charge, leaving finite predictions.
moments.takeaway: QED becomes computable. Three independent paths to the same theory — a sign that the theory is robust.

moments.title: Feynman diagrams enter physics
moments.body:
Feynman's diagrams — pictures of particles propagating and interacting at vertices — provide an intuitive bookkeeping for QED calculations. Every diagram corresponds to a mathematical contribution to the scattering amplitude.

The diagrams become the universal language of particle physics. They are adopted, with extensions, for QCD, electroweak theory, and ultimately the Standard Model.
moments.takeaway: A pictorial calculus replaces pages of algebra. Particle physics has its visual vocabulary.

moments.title: Nobel Prize
moments.body:
The 1965 Nobel Prize in Physics is shared by Tomonaga, Schwinger and Feynman for QED. Dyson is not included — limited to three laureates per prize. Feynman gives an iconic Nobel lecture.

QED becomes the template for all subsequent quantum field theories.
moments.takeaway: Three nationalities, three independent solutions to the same problem, all honoured together.

now.title: QED today
now.body:
QED is the most precisely tested theory in physics. The electron's anomalous magnetic moment (g-2) is predicted by QED and measured experimentally to about 12 significant figures — agreement is essentially perfect. (A small experimental-theoretical tension in muon g-2 is currently the subject of intense investigation.)

QED is the working model for all interactions of charged particles with light. It is also the model for how quantum field theories should be constructed — and was extended to QCD (the strong force) and electroweak theory.
now.open_questions: What's the source of the muon g-2 discrepancy? Are there particles or interactions beyond the Standard Model contributing to the precision tests of QED? Why are the fine-structure and other constants what they are?

reflection: Three physicists in three countries reached the same theory at nearly the same time after WWII. Tomonaga worked in war-damaged Tokyo with food rationing; Schwinger in Harvard; Feynman in Cornell. Independent simultaneous discovery often signals that an idea's time has arrived. How does science account for the role of historical timing in discovery?
